query: Consider the following context: Materials capable of withstanding extreme environments open promising opportunities for nuclear fusion reactors. In that context, which material can be used for interlayer materials between W and CuCrZr, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A nanocrystalline refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) — for example, a quinary alloy such as W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf — can serve as an effective interlayer between tungsten (W) and CuCrZr in fusion reactor applications by mitigating thermal expansion mismatches and enhancing irradiation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: As-fabricated nanocrystalline RHEA with fine grains and uniform elemental distribution.
generation.intervention: Introduce a thin film or foil of the selected RHEA as an interlayer when bonding tungsten and CuCrZr components.
generation.conditions: Extreme operating environments typical of nuclear fusion reactors, i.e., high cyclic thermal loads combined with high-energy particle irradiation (e.g., He implantation).
generation.structural_mediator: The nanocrystalline structure of the RHEA, with its stable grain boundaries and high chemical homogeneity, mediates the mismatch in thermal expansion and mechanical properties between the tungsten and CuCrZr layers.
generation.mechanism: The high configurational entropy in the RHEA stabilizes a single-phase structure under extreme conditions and its reported irradiation resistance helps prevent significant defect accumulation. This results in improved interfacial adhesion and a reduction in thermally induced stresses across the W/CuCrZr joint.
generation.predicted_outcome: The inclusion of the RHEA interlayer will yield improved joint integrity, reduced interfacial stress, and better overall durability under fusion reactor conditions compared to direct bonding of tungsten and CuCrZr.
generation.baseline: Conventional bonding without an interlayer suffers from issues such as poor adhesion and significant stress buildup due to thermal expansion differences.
generation.boundary: The advantages may diminish if the RHEA composition or interlayer thickness is not optimized, or if long-term degradation under reactor conditions occurs beyond current experimental observations.
generation.uncertainty: While there is supporting evidence for high thermal stability and irradiation resistance of RHEAs, the precise extent of stress mitigation at the W/CuCrZr interface and the long-term performance under operational reactor conditions remain to be experimentally quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate test specimens consisting of tungsten, the RHEA interlayer, and CuCrZr. Subject these specimens to cyclic thermal loading and He ion irradiation in a simulated fusion reactor environment alongside control samples without the interlayer.
measurements: Interfacial bonding strength (e.g., via shear testing)
Thermal stress distribution (using digital image correlation or finite element analysis)
Microstructural analysis at the interfaces (via TEM/SEM before and after testing)
Irradiation-induced defect evolution and grain stability
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the specimens with the RHEA interlayer do not exhibit significantly improved bonding strength, reduced interfacial thermal stress, and enhanced microstructural stability under irradiation compared to controls, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract In the quest of new materials that can withstand severe irradiation and mechanical extremes for advanced applications ( e.g . fission & fusion reactors, space applications, etc.), design, prediction and control of advanced materials beyond current material designs become paramount. Here, through a combined experimental and simulation methodology, we design a nanocrystalline refractory high entropy alloy (RHEA) system. Compositions assessed under extreme environments and in situ electron-microscopy reveal both high thermal stability and radiation resistance. We observe grain refinement under heavy ion irradiation and resistance to dual-beam irradiation and helium implantation in the form of low defect generation and evolution, as well as no detectable grain growth. The experimental and modeling results—showing a good agreement—can be applied to design and rapidly assess other alloys subjected to extreme environmental conditions. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Power stations

High thermal stability

The synthesized quinary W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf RHEA shows high thermal stability in terms of grain coarsening. Even though there was an increase in the grain size during He implantation, the material preserved its nano-crystallinity and showed only approximately 10 nm change in grain size after ~8.45 at.% He implantation. The previously studied quaternary W-Ta-Cr-V RHEA demonstrated a similar thermal stability regarding grain morphology [22] . One of the properties that distinguishes this quinary W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf RHEA from the previously studied RHEAs is the grain refinement observed during dual-beam irradiation. Grain refinement was observed before in other materials [32] . Two main suggested mechanisms are discussed in the literature: (i) defect clusters produced during irradiation can migrate to sub-grain boundaries and form cell structures that lead to small grain formation [32] and (ii) cascades that are larger than the grain size can form stacking faults across the grain breaking it into two separate crystalline structures (observed in FCC material) [33] .
